content: 1. Many individuals may not be aware that they are at risk for certain infections, and relying solely on a screening approach based on medical history may fail to identify a significant number of cases. 2. Provider-initiated testing and counseling (PITC) for HIV has shown high acceptance rates in antenatal care (ANC) and tuberculosis (TB) settings. 3. Offering partner testing for individuals with hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) can yield the highest possible detection rates, but there is a need to address reluctance in providing partner or index partner testing. 4. Community-based testing services should be made accessible in settings that are acceptable and convenient for key and vulnerable populations. These services should offer flexible hours, walk-in options, or same-day appointments to improve accessibility. 5. It is essential to involve affected populations, including adolescents, in the design, delivery, and evaluation of testing services to ensure these programs meet their needs. 6. Concerns about stigma, such as fear of being seen by older relatives, neighbors, or family friends while attending viral hepatitis or HIV services, must be addressed to encourage testing. 7. Testing programs for key populations should emphasize the World Health Organization’s (WHO) “5 Cs”: consent, confidentiality, counseling, correct results, and connection to comprehensive prevention, care, and treatment. 8. Community-based and rapid testing for HBV and HCV can improve the likelihood of key populations, such as prisoners, receiving their results. However, testing in certain populations, such as in prisons, may increase the risk of stigmatization. 9. Estimating the costs of hepatitis testing programs can be challenging due to variations between countries and program types. Factors influencing costs include personnel, recurrent costs (e.g., test kits, supplies), capital expenses (e.g., office space, equipment), and the ease of reaching different populations. 10. Standardized cost estimation approaches involve identifying costs incurred by healthcare providers, including personnel, materials (e.g., test kits, reagents, sterile equipment), and training and supervision of testing providers. 11. Community-based screening and treatment strategies, such as those implemented in The Gambia and Senegal, have demonstrated cost-effectiveness, with incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) well within acceptable thresholds. 12. Testing for couples and partners, particularly in antenatal care settings, provides an opportunity to integrate concurrent HBV testing for partners of women with chronic HBV or HCV infection. 13. Adolescents in high HBV-prevalence settings may require testing, particularly those exposed perinatally or through early childhood, as well as those who acquire HBV sexually or through injecting drug use. Perinatally infected adolescents urgently need diagnosis and linkage to care. 14. Universal HBV immunization, including a birth dose within 24 hours of birth, is critical for preventing mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HBV. However, economic and logistical constraints have hindered implementation in many countries. 15. Infants born to mothers diagnosed with HBV or HCV should be routinely followed up and offered early infant diagnosis (EID). Those diagnosed with HBV or HCV should be monitored for liver disease progression and treated when necessary. 16. Pediatric case finding is essential to address gaps in follow-up for infants and children exposed to HBV or HCV. This can be achieved through routine provider-initiated testing and counseling (PITC) in healthcare facilities and testing family members of index cases. 17. HBV and HCV testing services for infants should aim to identify infected individuals as early as possible to enable monitoring, treatment, and vaccination of household contacts. 18. In high-prevalence settings, HBV and HCV testing for mothers and infants should be routinely available through various services, including child health clinics, immunization programs, and services for hospitalized or vulnerable children. 19. Testing family members of HBV-positive parents or close household contacts is a priority to close gaps in HBV testing and documentation. 20. Testing strategies for HBV and HCV should include targeted risk-based screening for high-risk populations, such as people who inject drugs (PWID), men who have sex with men (MSM), sex workers, healthcare workers, and individuals attending viral hepatitis or HIV care services. 21. The majority of individuals with HCV infection are unaware of their status, often presenting with advanced disease. Low rates of diagnosis and poor linkage to care remain significant barriers to effective management. 22. Hepatitis B and C testing and diagnosis are critical entry points for prevention and treatment cascades. Testing identifies those who are positive, links them to care, and provides opportunities for counseling and treatment initiation. 23. Testing also identifies individuals who are negative, allowing for hepatitis B vaccination and implementation of prevention measures to reduce risk behaviors. 24. There are three main approaches to HCV screening: targeted risk factor-based screening, general population screening, and birth cohort screening. Each approach has its own benefits, harms, and cost-effectiveness considerations. 25. Targeted risk factor-based screening focuses on high-risk groups, such as PWID, prisoners, migrants, MSM, and sex workers, who are at higher risk of infection compared to the general population.
